## 1. Introduction (10 points)

::: callout-note
## Requirements

- State which dataset you chose and why
- Describe the dataset: source, size (rows × columns), key variables, time period
- State 2–3 specific questions you will explore
- Discuss data provenance: who collected this data, when, and for what purpose
:::

```{r}
#| label: load-data
url  <- "https://d37ci6vzurychx.cloudfront.net/trip-data/yellow_tripdata_2024-01.parquet"
dest <- "yellow_tripdata_2024-01.parquet"
if (!file.exists(dest)) download.file(url, dest, mode = "wb")

df_full <- arrow::read_parquet(dest)

set.seed(123)
df <- df_full |>
  dplyr::slice_sample(n = 50000) |>
  # TLC timestamps are local NYC clock times stored without a time zone; keep them
  # as-is (UTC label) so R does not shift them by the computer's time zone
  mutate(across(c(tpep_pickup_datetime, tpep_dropoff_datetime), ~ lubridate::with_tz(.x, "UTC")))
glimpse(df)
```

> *This is a dataset containing information about taxi trips taken in NYC during 2024. It is a 50000 x 19 dataset, containing variables such as the amount paid for the taxi fare and tip, the number of passengers, pickup and dropoff, and more. This data was collected by the NYC Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC) for the purpose of making data-driven insights about trip data. While there are a lot of things that could be explored with this data, I will focus on figuring out peak taxi hours, a potential correlation between passenger amount trip distance, and tipping behaviors across trip duration.*

## 2. Data Quality Assessment (15 points)

::: callout-note
## Requirements

- Report missing values per column (counts AND percentages)
- Identify data type issues (columns needing conversion)
- Check for impossible or suspicious values
- Document every cleaning step with justification
- Include before/after summary (e.g., row counts)
:::

### Missing Values

```{r}
#| label: missing-values
n_before <- nrow(df); p_before <- ncol(df)

missing_tbl <- df |>
  summarise(across(everything(), ~ sum(is.na(.x)))) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "column", values_to = "n_missing") |>
  mutate(pct_missing = round(100 * n_missing / nrow(df), 2)) |>
  arrange(desc(n_missing))
missing_tbl
```

> *The missing values appear to be systematic. The amount of missing values for the affected columns is the exact same, which implies that this was due to the type of vendor or trip that reports this data.*

### Data Type Checks

```{r}
#| label: data-types
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    payment_type = factor(payment_type, levels = 0:6,
      labels = c("Flex fare", "Credit card", "Cash", "No charge",
                 "Dispute", "Unknown", "Voided")),
    RatecodeID = factor(RatecodeID, levels = c(1:6, 99),
      labels = c("Standard", "JFK", "Newark", "Nassau/Westchester",
                 "Negotiated", "Group", "Unknown")),
    VendorID = factor(VendorID),
    store_and_fwd_flag = factor(store_and_fwd_flag)
  )
sapply(df, class)
```

> **The pickup and dropoff columns were already stored as datetimes, so no conversion was needed. Four columns were stored as integers or characters but are really categories: `payment_type`, `RatecodeID`, `VendorID`, and `store_and_fwd_flag`. I converted them to factors with readable labels so they are treated as categories and not as numbers in summaries and plots.*

### Suspicious Values

```{r}
#| label: suspicious-values
df <- df |>
  mutate(
    trip_minutes = as.numeric(difftime(tpep_dropoff_datetime, tpep_pickup_datetime, units = "mins")),
    mph = trip_distance / (trip_minutes / 60)
  )

outside_jan <- !(year(df$tpep_pickup_datetime) == 2024 & month(df$tpep_pickup_datetime) == 1)

suspicious <- tibble(
  check = c("pickup outside January 2024", "distance <= 0", "distance > 100 mi",
            "fare <= 0", "fare > $500", "negative tip", "duration <= 0",
            "duration > 180 min", "speed > 80 mph", "passengers 0 or > 6",
            "total < fare"),
  n = c(
    sum(outside_jan),
    sum(df$trip_distance <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$trip_distance > 100, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$fare_amount <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$fare_amount > 500, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$tip_amount < 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$trip_minutes <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$trip_minutes > 180, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$mph > 80, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$passenger_count == 0 | df$passenger_count > 6, na.rm = TRUE),
    sum(df$total_amount < df$fare_amount, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
)
suspicious
```

> *Several impossible or implausible values appear. The most common are zero-distance trips (984), zero or negative fares (672), and passenger counts of 0 or above 6 (543). Smaller numbers of trips have a dropoff at or before pickup (20), run longer than 3 hours (24), imply speeds above 80 mph (17), or have a negative tip (2). No pickups fall outside January 2024 and none exceed 100 miles or $500. I removed all of these rows (see the cleaning summary below), since they are errors, cancellations, or meter problems and would distort averages and correlations. The check for total below fare (625 rows) was not used for removal, because totals can be lower than the fare when a discount or adjustment applies.*

### Cleaning Summary

```{r}
#| label: cleaning
bad <- with(df,
  outside_jan |
  is.na(trip_distance) | trip_distance <= 0 | trip_distance > 100 |
  fare_amount <= 0 | fare_amount > 500 |
  tip_amount < 0 |
  trip_minutes <= 0 | trip_minutes > 180 |
  mph > 80 |
  is.na(passenger_count) | passenger_count < 1 | passenger_count > 6)

sum(bad)  # total rows removed

df_clean <- df |>
  filter(!coalesce(bad, TRUE)) |>
  mutate(
    pickup_hour = hour(tpep_pickup_datetime),
    pickup_wday = wday(tpep_pickup_datetime, label = TRUE, week_start = 1),
    day_type    = if_else(wday(tpep_pickup_datetime, week_start = 1) >= 6, "Weekend", "Weekday"),
    tip_pct     = 100 * tip_amount / fare_amount,
    dur_bin     = cut(trip_minutes, breaks = c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20, 30, 60, 180),
                      labels = c("<5", "5-10", "10-15", "15-20", "20-30", "30-60", "60+"))
  )

cat("Before:", n_before, "x", p_before, "| After:", nrow(df_clean), "x", ncol(df_clean))
```

> *I removed rows that were impossible or extremely implausible, plus rows with missing passenger count (which also covers the other four systematically missing columns). I also added derived columns: trip duration in minutes, speed in mph, pickup hour, day of week, weekday/weekend, tip percentage, and a duration bin. Counts below come from the suspicious-values table; a row can fall into more than one category, so the counts do not sum to the total removed.*

| Cleaning Step | Rows/Values Affected | Justification |
|----|----|----|
| Pickup outside January 2024 | 0 | Data file is for January 2024; stray timestamps are errors |
| Missing passenger count (and 4 other fields) | 2,349 | Cannot reasonably impute; systematic missingness |
| Distance <= 0 or > 100 mi | 984 | Zero-distance trips are likely cancellations; >100 mi is implausible for NYC taxis |
| Fare <= 0 or > $500 | 672 | Non-positive fares are voids or errors; extreme values are likely data-entry mistakes |
| Duration <= 0 or > 180 min | 44 | Dropoff before pickup is impossible; 3+ hours suggests a meter left running |
| Speed > 80 mph | 17 | Not realistic for city driving |
| Negative tip | 2 | Tips cannot be negative |
| Passengers 0 or > 6 | 543 | A standard NYC taxi seats at most 5-6 |

> Before cleaning: 50,000 rows × 19 columns \| After cleaning: 45,927 rows × 26 columns (4,073 rows removed; the 7 extra columns are the derived variables)

## 3. Univariate Analysis (15 points)

::: callout-note
## Requirements

- For at least 3 numeric variables: report center (mean/median), spread (SD/IQR), shape (skewness), and outliers
- For at least 2 categorical variables: report level counts and proportions
- Include at least 2 visualizations (histograms, bar charts, or similar)
- Interpret each visualization in prose
:::

### Numeric Variables

```{r}
#| label: numeric-summary
vars <- c("trip_distance", "fare_amount", "tip_amount", "trip_minutes")

skew <- function(x) mean((x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE))^3, na.rm = TRUE) / sd(x, na.rm = TRUE)^3

df_clean |>
  summarise(across(all_of(vars), list(
    mean = ~mean(.x, na.rm = TRUE), median = ~median(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = ~sd(.x, na.rm = TRUE), iqr = ~IQR(.x, na.rm = TRUE),
    skew = skew,
    n_outliers = ~sum(.x > quantile(.x, .75, na.rm = TRUE) + 1.5 * IQR(.x, na.rm = TRUE) |
                      .x < quantile(.x, .25, na.rm = TRUE) - 1.5 * IQR(.x, na.rm = TRUE), na.rm = TRUE)
  ), .names = "{.col}__{.fn}")) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = c("variable", "stat"), names_sep = "__") |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = stat, values_from = value) |>
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~round(.x, 2)))
```

> *All four variables are right-skewed, with means above medians and positive skewness (2.35 to 3.75). For trip distance, the median is 1.7 miles and the mean is 3.33, with 6,015 outliers by the 1.5 × IQR rule. Fares follow a similar pattern (median $12.80, mean $18.63) because fares are driven by distance and time. Tip amount has a median of $2.80, pulled down by the many $0 tips (mostly cash payments). Trip duration has a median of 11.7 minutes and an IQR of 11.6, with a long tail of slow trips. Most trips are short and cheap, with a minority of long trips (for example, airport rides) stretching the upper tail.*

```{r}
#| label: numeric-viz-1
#| fig-cap: "Most taxi trips are short: trip distance is strongly right-skewed"
ggplot(df_clean, aes(trip_distance)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 0.5, fill = "#0072B2", color = "white") +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 20)) +
  labs(title = "Most taxi trips are under 3 miles",
       x = "Trip distance (miles)", y = "Number of trips", caption = src)
```

> *The distribution is strongly right-skewed: the bulk of trips (about 73%) are under 3 miles, with a mode near 0.75 miles. A small secondary bump around 17-18 miles likely reflects airport trips. The axis is truncated at 20 miles for readability, but a few longer trips exist.*


### Categorical Variables

```{r}
#| label: categorical-summary
df_clean |> count(payment_type) |> mutate(prop = round(n / sum(n), 3))
df_clean |> count(pickup_wday) |> mutate(prop = round(n / sum(n), 3))
df_clean |> count(passenger_count) |> mutate(prop = round(n / sum(n), 3))
```

> *The categories are not balanced. Credit card is the dominant payment type (83.3% of trips), followed by cash (15.5%), and the other types are rare (about 1% combined). Passenger count is dominated by single riders (78.6%). Trips are spread across days of the week fairly evenly, though Wednesday has the most trips (17.0%) and Sunday the fewest (11.2%).*

```{r}
#| label: categorical-viz
#| fig-cap: "Credit cards account for most taxi payments"
df_clean |>
  count(payment_type) |>
  ggplot(aes(reorder(payment_type, n), n, fill = payment_type)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  coord_flip() +
  scale_fill_viridis_d() +
  labs(title = "Credit cards account for most payments",
       x = "Payment type", y = "Number of trips", caption = src)
```

> *Credit card payments outnumber all other types combined, with cash a distant second. This matters for the tipping analysis, because cash tips are typically not recorded in the data.*

## 4. Bivariate & Multivariate Analysis (20 points)

### Correlation Analysis

```{r}
#| label: correlation
#| fig-cap: "Fare, distance, and duration move together; passenger count is nearly unrelated to everything"
num_vars <- df_clean |>
  select(passenger_count, trip_distance, trip_minutes, fare_amount, tip_amount, tip_pct)

cor(num_vars, use = "complete.obs", method = "spearman") |>
  as.data.frame() |> rownames_to_column("var1") |>
  pivot_longer(-var1, names_to = "var2", values_to = "r") |>
  ggplot(aes(var1, var2, fill = r)) +
  geom_tile() +
  geom_text(aes(label = round(r, 2)), size = 3) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(limits = c(-1, 1)) +
  labs(title = "Fare, distance, and duration are strongly correlated",
       x = NULL, y = NULL, fill = "Spearman r", caption = src) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

> *I used Spearman correlation because the variables are skewed. The strongest correlations are among fare, distance, and duration (r ≈ 0.86 to 0.96), which is expected because the meter charges by both. Passenger count has near-zero correlation with the other variables (|r| < 0.05). Tip percentage is weakly negatively associated with trip variables (r ≈ -0.28 to -0.31), which is expected because short trips tend to have a minimum tip or rounded-up tip that is a large share of a small fare, while long trips' tips grow more slowly than their fares.*

### Relationship 1: Passenger count and trip distance

```{r}
#| label: passenger-distance-stats
cor(df_clean$passenger_count, df_clean$trip_distance, method = "spearman")

df_clean |>
  group_by(passenger_count) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_dist = mean(trip_distance), median_dist = median(trip_distance))
```

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-1
#| fig-cap: "Trip distance changes little with passenger count"
ggplot(df_clean, aes(factor(passenger_count), trip_distance)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#56B4E9", outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 15)) +
  labs(title = "Median trip distance is similar across passenger counts",
       x = "Number of passengers", y = "Trip distance (miles)", caption = src)
```

> *Passenger count is only weakly associated with trip distance (Spearman r = 0.03). Median distance ranges from 1.62 to 1.85 miles across passenger counts, and the boxes overlap heavily. With about 46,000 rows even a tiny correlation would be statistically detectable, so the practical effect size is what matters: here it is negligible. Groups with 5-6 passengers are small, so their boxes are less reliable.*

### Relationship 2: Tipping and trip duration

```{r}
#| label: tip-duration-stats
tip_cc <- df_clean |> filter(payment_type == "Credit card", tip_pct <= 100)

tip_cc |>
  group_by(dur_bin) |>
  summarise(n = n(), median_tip_pct = median(tip_pct), mean_tip_pct = mean(tip_pct),
            pct_zero_tip = 100 * mean(tip_amount == 0))
```

```{r}
#| label: bivariate-2
#| fig-cap: "Tip percentage by trip duration (credit-card trips)"
ggplot(tip_cc, aes(dur_bin, tip_pct)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6, outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0, 50)) +
  labs(title = "Tip percentage is highest on short trips and declines as trips get longer",
       x = "Trip duration (minutes)", y = "Tip (% of fare)", caption = src)
```

> *I restricted this analysis to credit-card trips, since cash tips are almost always recorded as $0 and would make riders look like non-tippers. Median tip percentage is 34.1% for trips under 5 minutes and 22.4% for trips of 30-60 minutes, so tip percentage is lower as trips get longer. Trips under 5 minutes may have many small fares where a minimum tip dominates. The 60+ minute group (median 11.4%, 42% with no tip) is small (375 trips) and likely includes unusual trips.*

```{r}
#| label: tip-scatter
#| fig-cap: "Tip percentage versus duration with trend line"
ggplot(tip_cc, aes(trip_minutes, tip_pct)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.05, color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_smooth(color = "#D55E00", se = FALSE) +
  coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 60), ylim = c(0, 50)) +
  labs(title = "Longer trips are not associated with higher tip percentages",
       x = "Trip duration (minutes)", y = "Tip (% of fare)", caption = src)
```

> *The trend line falls steeply over the first 10-15 minutes and then declines more gradually (Spearman r = -0.45 for credit-card trips). Tip percentage is clustered around 24-29% of the fare, consistent with the preset tip options on payment screens (often 20%, 25%, 30% of the total, which includes taxes and surcharges, so the share of the fare alone runs somewhat higher).*

### Faceted / Grouped Analysis

```{r}
#| label: faceted
#| fig-cap: "The passenger-distance link differs between standard and JFK trips"
df_clean |>
  filter(RatecodeID %in% c("Standard", "JFK")) |>
  ggplot(aes(factor(passenger_count), trip_distance)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "#56B4E9", outlier.alpha = 0.1) +
  facet_wrap(~RatecodeID, scales = "free_y") +
  labs(title = "JFK trips are much longer than standard trips at every passenger count",
       x = "Number of passengers", y = "Trip distance (miles)", caption = src)
```

> *Splitting by rate code reveals that JFK trips are far longer (median about 18 miles) than standard trips (median about 1.6 miles) at every passenger count, a difference the aggregate view blends together. Within each group, passenger count is still essentially unrelated to distance (Spearman r = 0.02 for Standard, -0.03 for JFK). This shows that the rate code (trip type) explains much more of the variation in distance than the number of passengers.*

### Confounding & Simpson's Paradox

```{r}
#| label: confounding
# Tip % vs. duration, by rate code
tip_cc |> group_by(RatecodeID) |>
  summarise(n = n(), r = cor(trip_minutes, tip_pct, method = "spearman"))

# Tip % by payment type (all trips)
df_clean |>
  filter(payment_type %in% c("Credit card", "Cash")) |>
  group_by(payment_type) |>
  summarise(n = n(), mean_tip_pct = mean(tip_pct), pct_zero_tip = 100 * mean(tip_amount == 0))
```

> *Payment type is a major confounder for tipping. Cash trips show a mean tip of 0% because cash tips are not recorded, while credit-card trips show 25.4%. If both were pooled, any pattern between tipping and trip duration would partly reflect the mix of payment types at different durations, not riders' behavior. Rate code is a second confounder: flat-rate JFK trips have long durations and large fares, so they can pull the overall relationship between duration and tip percentage. Within-group correlations are -0.43 for Standard and +0.06 for JFK versus -0.45 overall, so the direction does not meaningfully change when I control for rate code: the negative relationship comes almost entirely from Standard trips, which are the vast majority (JFK is near zero). This is confounding, not a strict Simpson's reversal.*


```{r}
#| label: peak-hours-table
df_clean |> count(pickup_hour, sort = TRUE) |> slice_head(n = 3)
```

> *Averaged per day so weekdays and weekends are comparable, weekday demand rises sharply in the morning, dips midday, and peaks between 5 and 7 PM (the busiest hour overall is 17:00, with 3,259 trips, just ahead of 18:00 with 3,233). Weekend demand starts later in the morning, peaks around 1 to 5 PM, and remains higher than weekdays late at night. This is consistent with commuting and evening activity driving weekday demand and nightlife driving weekend demand.*

```{r}
#| label: extra-viz-2
#| fig-cap: "Busiest period is weekday late afternoon"
df_clean |>
  count(pickup_wday, pickup_hour) |>
  ggplot(aes(pickup_hour, fct_rev(pickup_wday), fill = n)) +
  geom_tile() +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(labels = comma) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 23, 3)) +
  labs(title = "Weekday 4-7 PM is the busiest stretch",
       x = "Pickup hour (0-23)", y = "Day of week", fill = "Trips", caption = src)
```

> *The brightest cells are on Wednesday (then Tuesday and Thursday) between 5 and 7 PM, confirming the line chart's evening peak. The darkest cells are in the early morning (about 2-5 AM) on weekdays. Saturday and Sunday differ: they stay busy past midnight (Sunday 12 AM is one of the brighter early cells) and are quiet only around 5-6 AM.*

## 6. Ethical Reflection (10 points)

::: callout-note
## Requirements

- Assess representativeness: who is included in this dataset? Who is missing?
- Identify at least one finding that could be misleading without context
- Discuss what conclusions should NOT be drawn from this data
- Use "associated with" language, not causal claims
:::

### Representativeness

> *This dataset only represents trips taken in NYC yellow taxis during January 2024, and only the ones that were recorded by the taxi's metering system. Anyone who did not ride a yellow taxi is missing: people who used the subway, buses, Uber and Lyft, or green cabs, and people who could not afford or did not have access to a taxi. Taxi riders skew toward people who are traveling for work, going to the airport, or can pay for convenience, and trips are concentrated in Manhattan, so outer-borough residents are likely underrepresented. The data also describes trips, not people: one person who rides daily appears many times. January is a single cold winter month with no major holidays except New Year's, so seasonal patterns (summer tourism, for example) are absent. Finally, 2,349 trips (about 4.7% of the sample) were missing passenger count and four other fields, and I dropped them. If these trips differ systematically from the rest, my results would be biased. Conclusions about all New Yorkers, or about NYC transportation as a whole, would be wrong.*

### Potentially Misleading Findings

> *The biggest risk is the tipping result. Taken at face value, the data says cash riders tip 0% while credit-card riders tip 25.4% on average, and a careless reader could conclude that cash riders are stingy. In reality, cash tips are not recorded by the meter, so the 0% reflects missing measurement, not behavior. I would report tipping only for credit-card trips and say so explicitly. A second example is the fall in tip percentage with trip length (34.1% median for trips under 5 minutes versus 22.4% for 30-60 minutes). Someone might read this as "riders on long trips are less generous," but it may simply reflect that short trips have small fares where a minimum or rounded-up tip is a large share, and that the longest trips include airport trips with flat or negotiated pricing. I would present this as a pattern in percentages, alongside the dollar tip amount, which rises with trip length (Spearman r = 0.44). Lastly, the busiest hours I found apply to January weekdays and to trips picked up by yellow taxis only, so they should not be described as when "New York" travels.*

### What This Data Cannot Answer

> *First, this data cannot show that trip length causes lower tip percentages, or that payment type causes different tipping. We can only say that longer trips are associated with lower tip percentages among credit-card riders. Unmeasured factors such as rider income, trip purpose, mood, the driver's behavior, and the default tip options on the payment screen could all explain the pattern. Second, we cannot conclude that passenger count has no effect on how far people travel in general. We only found a near-zero association (r = 0.03) in January yellow-taxi trips, and the groups with 5 or 6 passengers are small. Third, we cannot generalize to other months, other years, or other ride services; the weekday evening peak and the airport trips seen here may look different in summer or in app-based rides. Fourth, because I removed about 8% of the sample as errors, any estimate depends on my cutoffs (for example 180 minutes and 80 mph), and different thresholds could change the numbers slightly.*

------------------------------------------------------------------------

## 7. Conclusion (10 points)

::: callout-note
## Requirements

- Summarize your top 3 findings with supporting evidence
- State what surprised you
- Propose 2–3 follow-up questions this EDA cannot answer but further analysis could
:::

### Top 3 Findings

1.  *Taxi demand peaks in the evening on weekdays. Averaged per day, weekday pickups are highest between 5 and 7 PM (the busiest hour overall is 17:00 with 3,259 trips), and Wednesday evenings are the busiest cells in the heatmap. Weekends start later, peak in the afternoon, and stay busier than weekdays after midnight.*
2.  *Passenger count is essentially unrelated to trip distance. The Spearman correlation is 0.03, median distance only ranges from 1.62 to 1.85 miles across passenger counts, and the result holds within both Standard and JFK trips. Rate code explains far more: JFK trips have a median of about 18 miles versus about 1.6 for Standard trips.*
3.  *Among credit-card trips, tip percentage is associated with shorter trips. Median tip is 34.1% for trips under 5 minutes versus 22.4% for 30-60 minutes (Spearman r = -0.45). This only holds for credit cards, since cash tips are recorded as $0 (mean tip 0% for cash versus 25.4% for credit card).*

### Surprises

> *I expected passenger count to have at least a small link to trip distance, and it was surprising how close to zero it was. I was also surprised that the evening peak was so clear on weekdays, with a lunchtime plateau rather than a sharp morning rush, and by how much the data cleaning mattered: a time zone shift in how R read the timestamps initially made the busiest hour look like noon, which would have been a wrong conclusion. Finally, about 8% of the sample had to be removed as impossible or missing, which was more than I expected for official data.*

### Follow-Up Questions

1.  *Do the weekday evening peak and the tipping patterns hold in other months? Repeating the analysis on the TLC files for July and October 2024 would show whether they are seasonal.*
2.  *Does pickup or dropoff location (borough or airport zone) explain the differences in tip percentage and trip length? Joining the location IDs to the TLC taxi zone lookup table would let us test this.*
3.  *Is the missing-data group (passenger count and four other fields missing together) systematically different, for example by vendor? Comparing fares, distances, and vendor IDs between those trips and the rest would show whether dropping them biased the results.*
